question: Explain the Singleton design pattern, its use case, and why it's sometimes considered an anti-pattern.

key_points: Singleton ensures a class has exactly one instance, with a global access point to it — used for shared resources like a config manager or connection pool
Criticism: it introduces global mutable state, making code harder to test (hard to substitute a mock/fake) and creating hidden dependencies between unrelated parts of the code
In multi-threaded contexts, naive Singleton implementations can have race conditions during lazy initialization if not made thread-safe
Modern alternative: dependency injection, passing the single shared instance explicitly rather than having classes reach out to a global
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Singleton pattern ensures a class has only one instance throughout the application, with some global point of access to it — commonly used for things like a configuration manager or a shared connection pool where having multiple instances would be wasteful or incorrect. It's often criticized as an anti-pattern because it introduces global mutable state, which makes unit testing harder since you can't easily substitute a fake or mock instance, and it creates hidden coupling — any code can reach into the singleton without that dependency being visible in a class's constructor or interface. A naive lazy-initialized Singleton can also have race conditions in multi-threaded code if not implemented carefully. Many modern codebases prefer dependency injection instead — creating one shared instance and explicitly passing it to whatever needs it — which keeps the same 'single instance' benefit while being far more testable.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to describe how they'd make a lazy-initialized Singleton thread-safe.

question: Explain the Observer design pattern and give a real-world example of its use.

key_points: Observer pattern: a subject maintains a list of dependents (observers) and notifies them automatically of any state changes
Decouples the subject from the specific observers — the subject doesn't need to know concrete details of who's listening, only that they implement a common notification interface
Real-world examples: DOM event listeners, React/Vue reactive state updates triggering re-renders, pub/sub messaging systems, model-view frameworks (MVC 'view' observing 'model' changes)
Trade-off: can make control flow harder to trace since a state change can trigger a cascade of updates in code that isn't visibly connected at the call site
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Observer pattern lets a subject maintain a list of dependent observers and automatically notify all of them whenever its state changes, without the subject needing to know any specifics about those observers beyond a common notification interface — this decouples the subject from whoever happens to be listening. A very familiar real-world example is DOM event listeners: clicking a button notifies all registered listener functions without the button needing to know what those callbacks do. React's state updates triggering component re-renders, and general pub/sub messaging systems, follow the same idea. The trade-off is that it can make control flow harder to trace, since a single state change can silently cascade into updates across several observers whose connection isn't visible just by reading the code at the point where the state changed.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to implement a minimal Observer pattern (subscribe/unsubscribe/notify) from scratch.

question: What is the Factory pattern, and when would you use it instead of directly instantiating a class with 'new'?

key_points: Factory pattern: encapsulates object creation logic in a dedicated method/class, rather than the caller directly calling a constructor
Useful when the exact class to instantiate depends on runtime conditions (e.g. different payment processor implementations based on config), or when construction involves non-trivial setup logic
Decouples calling code from concrete classes — callers depend only on a common interface/abstract type, making it easier to introduce new implementations without changing calling code
Reduces duplication if the same complex construction logic would otherwise be repeated across many call sites
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Factory pattern encapsulates the logic of creating an object inside a dedicated method or class, rather than having calling code directly instantiate a concrete class with 'new'. This is useful when the specific class to instantiate needs to be decided at runtime — for example, choosing between different payment processor implementations based on configuration — or when construction involves meaningful setup logic that shouldn't be duplicated everywhere an instance is needed. It also decouples calling code from concrete implementations: callers depend only on a common interface or abstract base type, so you can add a new implementation later without touching any of the existing call sites that create objects through the factory.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to distinguish Factory Method from Abstract Factory.

question: Explain the Strategy design pattern with an example.

key_points: Strategy pattern: defines a family of interchangeable algorithms/behaviors behind a common interface, and lets the algorithm be selected/swapped at runtime
The context class holds a reference to a strategy object and delegates the behavior to it, without knowing the concrete implementation
Avoids large conditional blocks (if/else or switch chains) picking behavior based on type — instead each behavior is its own class implementing the shared interface
Example: different sorting algorithms, different payment methods, or different compression algorithms all implementing a common interface, selected/injected based on context
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms or behaviors behind a common interface, letting the actual algorithm used be selected or swapped at runtime rather than hardcoded. A 'context' object holds a reference to a strategy object and delegates the actual work to it through the shared interface, without needing to know which concrete strategy is plugged in. A concrete example is a checkout system supporting multiple payment methods — credit card, PayPal, wallet — each implemented as a class conforming to a common PaymentStrategy interface with a 'pay' method; the checkout context just calls strategy.pay() without caring which one it actually is. This avoids a large if/else or switch statement branching on payment type scattered through the codebase, and makes adding a new payment method as simple as adding a new class.

follow_up_hint: Ask them how Strategy differs from simply passing a function/lambda as a parameter in a language that supports first-class functions.

question: What is the Decorator pattern, and how does it differ from simple inheritance for adding behavior?

key_points: Decorator wraps an object to add behavior/responsibilities dynamically at runtime, without modifying the original class or requiring a fixed subclass for every combination
Decorators implement the same interface as the object they wrap, so they can be stacked/composed and used interchangeably with the original

Inheritance defines behavior additions statically at compile time and can lead to a combinatorial explosion of subclasses if you need every combination of optional behaviors (e.g. CoffeeWithMilk, CoffeeWithMilkAndSugar, ...)
Real-world example: Java I/O streams (wrapping a FileInputStream with a BufferedInputStream, then a GZIPInputStream), or middleware layers each adding a responsibility
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Decorator pattern wraps an object with another object that implements the same interface, adding extra behavior around calls to the wrapped object, and this can be done dynamically at runtime rather than being fixed at compile time. Because a decorator implements the same interface as what it wraps, decorators can be stacked in any combination, and callers can't tell the difference between the wrapped and unwrapped object. Inheritance, by contrast, bakes in behavior additions statically through subclassing, and if you need every combination of several optional behaviors, you end up needing a subclass for each combination — a classic example is a Coffee base class needing CoffeeWithMilk, CoffeeWithSugar, CoffeeWithMilkAndSugar subclasses, which explodes combinatorially, whereas decorators let you compose MilkDecorator and SugarDecorator around a base Coffee object flexibly. Java's I/O stream classes, where you wrap a FileInputStream with a BufferedInputStream and then a GZIPInputStream, are a well-known real example.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to implement a simple Decorator pattern for adding logging around an existing service's method calls.
